name: Interview behavioural questions, set 6
description: Spoken behavioural questions with model answers and rubrics: a difficult colleague, too much to do, unfair criticism, study or work, a losing run, closing questions, a second try and a result too good. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: a colleague you found difficult.

widget.prompt: Tell me about a time you worked with someone you found difficult.
widget.model: In my second year I worked weekend shifts at a busy café near campus. The shift lead often redid my tasks without a word, and twice she moved my break with no notice. I found it frustrating, and at first I assumed she did not trust me. So I asked her for ten minutes after a quiet Sunday close. It turned out the owner had blamed her for a stock shortage the summer before, after a new starter miscounted. From her side, checking everyone's work was how she protected herself. That was fair, and it changed what I did. I started writing my stock counts on the shared sheet with the time and my initials, and I sent her any swap requests a day ahead in one message. Within a month she stopped redoing my counts. By spring she asked me to train two new starters on the stock routine. I learned to ask what pressure someone is under before deciding they are difficult.

rubric.text: Describes what the person did, as behaviour rather than character
Puts the other person's view fairly, with the reason behind it
What you changed in your own conduct, specifically
The outcome, with a concrete sign that it worked
No blame or put-down of the other person
Under 300 words, told in the order it happened

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: The interviewer wants to see you work with people you would not choose. Describe behaviour, not character, and put the other side's view fairly. Then show what you changed in your own conduct and how you knew it worked.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: too many things at once.

widget.prompt: Describe a time you had too many things to do. How did you choose?
widget.model: In the spring of my second year, one week held four things. There was a probability problem sheet worth 10 per cent of a module, a group presentation on the Friday, my robotics society's competition entry due on the Saturday, and two shifts at my part-time job. I had about 30 free hours and needed roughly 42. I listed each task with its hours, its deadline and what missing it would cost. My rule was to rank by the cost of a miss for each hour of work. The problem sheet and the presentation came first, because they counted towards my degree and others relied on the presentation. The robotics entry mattered to the team, so I cut my part to the wiring only I could do. I asked a teammate to take the testing, and told him on the Monday, not the Friday. I swapped one shift with a colleague and told my manager a week ahead. Everything went in on time, and our entry placed fourth of eleven.

rubric.text: Lists the competing tasks, with hours or deadlines
States the rule you ranked them by
Names what you dropped or cut back, plainly
Says whom you told and when
The outcome of each main task
Under 300 words, told in the order it happened

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: This question tests how you decide, not how hard you work. Show the list with hours, state the rule you ranked by, and name what you cut. Telling people early is part of the answer, so say whom you told and when.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: criticism you thought unfair.

widget.prompt: Tell me about criticism you thought was unfair.
widget.model: I gave a talk on Markov chains to my university's maths society. Afterwards the society's president told me it was aimed at nobody: too hard for first-years and too slow for finalists. I thought that was unfair. I had asked about the audience in advance and been told it was mixed, and twenty people had stayed for questions. That evening I went through all 31 feedback forms. Most were positive, but nine said they were lost by the second example, and all nine were first-years. So part of the criticism was right. I had pitched the middle of the talk at the wrong level, even if the whole talk was not aimed at nobody. I rewrote it with one worked example first and the harder material marked as optional at the end. I gave it again the next term, and of 27 forms, two said they were lost. I thanked the president and told her what I had changed.

rubric.text: States the criticism as it was said
Gives your reason for thinking it unfair, without attacking the critic
Names the part that was right, with evidence
What you changed because of it, specifically
The result of the change, with a number
Under 300 words, told in the order it happened

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: The interviewer is testing whether you can learn from feedback you dislike. Say why it felt unfair, then find the part that was right with evidence. A change and its measured result show you used it.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: an internship before more study.

widget.prompt: Why an internship now, rather than more study first?
widget.model: I have weighed a master's first, so I will say what each would give me. More study would deepen my statistics, especially time series and stochastic calculus, and it would keep doors open. But there are three things I can only learn on a desk. One is how decisions are made with a price moving and a clock running, which no exam reproduces. Another is what the data really looks like: gaps, bad ticks and the cost of every trade. The third is which of my skills matter most in practice, which tells me what any further study should cover. My final-year modules already give me the basics a desk expects: probability, regression and programming in Python. So my choice is the internship now. If it shows me I need a master's, I will apply knowing which courses I need and why, which makes the degree worth more. If it shows I can learn on the job, I will have saved a year.

rubric.text: Says what further study would add, fairly
Two or more things you can learn only on a desk
Shows you already have the basics the role needs
Makes a clear choice and gives its reason
Says how the internship would shape any later study
Under 300 words

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: The interviewer wants a decision, not a defence of one path. Give further study its due, then name what only a desk can teach. End on a clear choice and how it would shape what you study later.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: five losses in a row.

widget.prompt: In a trading game you have lost on five trades in a row. Talk me through what you check before the sixth. You have two minutes.
widget.model: First I would separate luck from error. Suppose I believed my trades win 55 per cent of the time. Then five losses in a row has chance 0.45 to the fifth, about 1.8 per cent, for any five trades I pick in advance. But over a game of 40 trades, a run of five losses somewhere happens in about one game in three. So the streak alone does not prove I am wrong. Next I would check each of the five trades against the price I traded at. Was I buying above where the market settled, or selling below it, every time? If all five errors point the same way, my estimate of fair value is off, and I would work it out again from scratch. Then I would look at size. Before the sixth trade I would halve my size until that check is done, so a broken estimate cannot cost much. Finally, I would say what would change my mind: two more losses at half size and I stop trading that market.

rubric.text: Separates luck from error before acting
Puts a number on the chance of five losses at your assumed edge
Checks each trade's price against a fair value
Changes size by a stated rule before the sixth trade
Says what further result would make you stop
Short enough for two minutes, with the checks in a stated order

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: The interviewer is testing whether a bad run changes your process or only your mood. Put a number on the run at your assumed edge, then check the prices for a pattern. Cut size by a rule and say what would make you stop.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: your questions for the interviewer.

widget.prompt: It is the end of the day and I ask whether you have any questions for me. What do you ask, and why?
widget.model: I would ask two questions, both about your own experience, because the careers pages already cover the programme and the training. First: think of the last graduate who did really well in their first year on your team. What did they do in their first three months that others did not? I would ask that because it tells me what good looks like from the person who judges it, and I can act on it from my first day. Second: what about this job did you find harder than you expected when you started? I would ask that because it shows me the part of the work a job description leaves out, and how you dealt with it, which tells me what to prepare before I start. I would not ask about pay, hours or the training schedule here, because those are published or are better asked of the recruiting team. If there were time, I would follow up on whichever answer surprised me most.

rubric.text: Two questions, each one only this interviewer could answer
A reason given for each question
Each question is open: yes, no or one fact would not answer it
Shows how you would use each answer, for example from the first day
Says what you would not ask here, and why
Under 300 words

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: Your questions show what you value and how prepared you are. Ask what only this person knows, such as their own experience, and say why each answer matters to you. Leave published facts and pay for another channel.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: turned down last year.

widget.prompt: You applied to us last year and were turned down. What is different this time?
widget.model: Last year I reached the second round and was turned down after the live coding interview. The feedback was one line, but it matched my own sense: my solution worked, yet I wrote it in silence and could not explain its cost when asked. So the gap was explaining code as I write it, not writing it. Since then I have done three things. I solved two problems a week aloud with a friend on a shared screen, and she counted the steps she could not follow. Over fourteen sessions that count fell from about six a problem to one. I learned to state the running time before I type, and I now check it against a timed run. And I took a tutoring shift for first-year programming, which makes me explain other people's code every week. I am applying again because my reasons for wanting the role have not changed, and the weakness that stopped me is measurably smaller.

rubric.text: Names the gap plainly, in your own words
What you did about it, with at least two actions
Evidence of improvement, as a measured number
No blame on the process, the interviewers or luck
Says why you still want this role
Under 300 words, told in the order it happened

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: A second application is judged on what changed. Name the gap without excuses, then show what you did with numbers that moved. Ending on why you still want the role shows the change was aimed at it.

items.question: Answer aloud, then type it: a result that looks too good.

widget.prompt: Your result looks too good. Convince me it is not a bug.
widget.model: My project predicted which students would drop a statistics module, from their first three weeks of online activity. It scored 91 per cent accuracy, which I also found suspicious. I ran three checks, in order. First, leakage: I listed when each input was recorded and confirmed that none came after week three. That found one bug, a forum count that ran to the end of term. Removing it dropped accuracy to 84 per cent. Second, a baseline: always predicting that a student stays scored 80 per cent, so the model's edge was four points, not eleven. Third, held-out data: I had kept the next year's cohort of 400 students untouched, and on it the model scored 83 per cent. The standard error there is about 2 points, so that is one and a half standard errors above the baseline. What still worries me is drift, because the module changed its coursework that year and three points may not last.

rubric.text: Checks for leakage first and says what it found
Compares with a simple baseline, giving both numbers
Tests on data held out from the start, with its result
Says how large the remaining edge is against its noise
Names what would still worry you
The checks come in a stated order, each with what it showed

feedback.correct: Compare your answer with the model and tick the rubric.
feedback.generic: Open the model answer and mark each rubric line.

explain.text: The interviewer wants a method for doubting your own result. Check leakage first, then a simple baseline, then data you never touched, and say what each showed. Size what is left against its noise, and name what still worries you.
